research.title: HPC Strategies for Parallel Implementations of Tensor Decompositions
research.short_title: tSVDm: exact multi-GPU star-M tensor SVD (t-SVDM / t-SVDMII)
research.lab: MATRIX Lab, Department of Computational and Data Sciences, IISc Bangalore (group of Prof. Phani Motamarri; ACM Gordon Bell Prize-winning lab)
research.collaboration: Argonne National Laboratory (Vishwas Rao; POD-DEIM in the star-M product framework) -- application target; nature of the collaboration to be confirmed before it is stated as active joint work
research.code_timeline: Implementation started mid-June 2026; first measured campaign Aug 2026; NCCL transport and generated DCT Sep 2026; report 18 Sep 2026.
research.codebase: tSVDm: C++17/CUDA 12.6 + OpenMPI + NCCL 2.23.4; cuBLAS/cuSOLVER; NumPy/SciPy reference; MATLAB cross-validation harness; SLURM campaign scripts; Python analysis (parse_results.py, make_report.py, audit_runs.py)
research.machine: Matrix CDS cluster, IISc: 2 nodes x (48 Xeon Gold 6248R cores, 579 GB RAM, 8x Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB), NVLink 2.0 intra-node, 100 Gbps ConnectX-5 InfiniBand inter-node
research.one_liner: Designed and built tSVDm, a C++/CUDA + MPI + NCCL implementation of the star-M tensor decompositions t-SVDM and t-SVDMII on 16 V100 GPUs, proved it exact against the published theorems, and measured it phase-by-phase against an independent CPU/MPI reference: 1.5-8.8x faster on large frontal faces, near-perfect strong and weak scaling, and the only implementation that completes a 4096^3 (512 GB) tensor.

bullets.text: Designed and implemented tSVDm, a distributed C++17/CUDA implementation of the star-M tensor decompositions t-SVDM (uniform rank k) and t-SVDMII (global energy threshold eta) for third- and higher-order tensors in FP32 and FP64, one MPI rank per GPU, on 2 nodes x 8 Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB.

Factorised every frontal face with an exact economy SVD (cuSOLVER gesvdj, one-sided Jacobi) issued one face per call across concurrent CUDA streams, each with its own handle and workspace, because t-SVDMII's threshold is a global order statistic that no truncated or randomized per-face factorisation can reproduce; faces with m < p are handled by a bank-conflict-free batched tiled transpose.

Implemented the mode-N transform as a bandwidth-optimal NCCL point-to-point ring over NVLink (ring order 0-3-2-1-5-6-7-4 measured as the NV2 Hamiltonian cycle), with in-place strided cuBLAS GEMMs and the next round's exchange posted before the current GEMM, after diagnosing that CUDA-aware MPI aborts on the cluster (UCX built without CUDA).

Replaced the stored n x n DCT-II operator with an on-the-fly generator (column blocks from a 4n-entry cosine table with integer argument reduction q = k(2l+1) mod 4n), cutting the operand from O(n^2) to a constant and making 256x256x131072 and 128x128x524288 runnable (161.8 s / 287.6 s FP32 on 8 GPUs) where a dense DCT would need 64 GB to 1 TB and the CPU reference cannot run at all.

Found and fixed a correctness bug in the first campaign where the t-SVDMII threshold compared local against global energy and never fired on P > 1 ranks; rewrote threshold selection as bisection on tau^2 with one scalar MPI_Allreduce per step (about 55 steps), returning the same threshold as the global sort and making tau^2 and eta_achieved bit-identical across 1, 2, 4 and 8 GPUs.

Verified correctness against the theory rather than asserting it: the Theorem 4 / Corollary 6 energy identity holds to 8.7e-15 in FP64 (2.3e-5 in FP32), the Eckart-Young equalities of Theorems 10 and 11 match measured reconstruction error to every printed digit in FP64 and six significant digits in FP32, and across all 87 GPU runs the achieved retention never fell below the 0.99 target (max overshoot 5.4e-5).

Cross-validated semantics against a NumPy/SciPy oracle (306 of 309 checks pass, none fail; DCT agrees with scipy.fft.dct to 2.7e-15) and element-wise against Newman's MATLAB star-M-opt package, and confirmed agreement with an independently written CPU/MPI implementation (StarMpiSVD): identical implicit rank 201,984 at 4096x4096x64 FP64 and tau^2 within 4.1e-5 relative.

Engineered three memory placements behind one code path (device-resident, pinned-host-streamed, and recompute-singular-values-then-refactorise) plus a row-blocked in-place out-of-core TTM, with every placement decision MPI_MAX-reduced to avoid ring deadlock; this ran 4096^3 FP64 (512 GB tensor + 1 TB factors) in 2719 s on 16 GPUs, a configuration that OOM-kills the CPU reference.

Benchmarked a 35-configuration matrix in both precisions against StarMpiSVD (CPU/MPI, MKL, Intel MPI) node-for-node under a stated fairness protocol (same transform, truncation criterion, warm-up and 5 timed runs, --exclusive nodes): 1.5x to 8.8x faster end-to-end where frontal faces are >= 1024 (8.76x at 4096x4096x64 FP64, 4.24x at 2048^3 FP64), and quantified the small-face regime (0.23-0.86x) where per-face gesvdj launches cannot fill a V100.

Measured strong scaling on a 1024^3 tensor from 1 to 16 GPUs across two nodes: 7.89x on 8 GPUs (efficiency 0.986) and 14.20x on 16 GPUs (0.888) in FP32; 15.77x on 16 GPUs in FP64 (0.985), and correctly attributed the FP64 efficiency > 1 at P = 2..12 to an out-of-core memory-regime change at the P = 1 baseline rather than superlinear scaling.

Measured weak scaling at 512 frontal faces of 512x512 per GPU (Gustafson-Barsis): scaled efficiency 0.985 within one node and 0.89 across two nodes (16 GPUs) against 0.70-0.77 for the CPU reference over the same unit range, and modelled the one-node-to-two-node step as the ring's fixed InfiniBand penalty per block.

Placed every configuration on a V100 roofline from nominal FLOP and HBM byte counts: all sit 18-5044x above the ridge point (compute-bound), attaining 0.1-25% of peak (31.4 TFLOP/s on 8 GPUs at 128x128x524288 FP32), and diagnosed the gap as kernel-launch and Jacobi-iteration latency rather than bandwidth; derived an NVLink/InfiniBand interconnect roof for the ring TTM.

Evaluated cuSOLVER gesvdaStridedBatched as an alternative face solver: 9.4x (FP32) to 14.2x (FP64) faster on the SVD phase at 128x128 faces, turning a 0.86x slowdown into a 6.6x end-to-end speedup, with bit-identical tau^2 in FP64; kept it optional because its normal-equations residual (1e-3 in FP32) fails the accuracy gate, and worked around its 32-bit workspace ceiling by adaptive sub-batching.

Practised numerical hygiene throughout: double-precision accumulators for every Frobenius reduction regardless of working precision, no --use_fast_math, allocation hoisted out of timed regions, position-addressable (splitmix64-hashed) data generation so the tensor is bitwise identical at every rank count, and an untimed accuracy gate that must pass before any timed job is submitted.

Documented two defects in the published pseudocode of Kilmer-Horesh-Avron-Newman (2019): Algorithm 3 compares unsquared singular values against a squared threshold, and Theorem 11 as printed omits the 1/|c|^2 factor present in Newman's thesis; the implementation works in squares and carries the factor.

research.future_work: Other machines/device generations; real data with decaying spectra (simulation output, image/video); learned transforms via variable projection (Newman-Keegan star-M-opt); POD-DEIM reduced-order modelling in the star-M framework (Rao et al.); TuckerMPI-style general compression; grouping small faces or using gesvda where residual permits; FFT-based O(n log n) DCT.

projects.name: DFT-FE to CLAP GEMM integration
projects.subtitle: Routing DFT-FE's level-3 BLAS calls through the CLAP library (ParaS ecosystem) with a verification and measurement layer
projects.date_note: 2026, MATRIX Lab side project; exact months not recorded in the source document
projects.context: MATRIX Lab side project alongside the thesis (DFT-FE is the lab's Gordon Bell Prize-winning DFT code)
projects.one_liner: Replaced all eight xgemm overloads in DFT-FE's BLASWrapper (host and device) with CLAP calls behind a configure-time switch, keeping upstream bit-identical when CLAP is off and shipping a verification/statistics layer so the substitution can be measured, not just compiled.

bullets.text: Routed DFT-FE's eight xgemm overloads (float/double/complex, host and device memory spaces) through CLAP's four IBlasBackend GEMM entry points while preserving every public signature so callers across DFT-FE are untouched.

Made the substitution reversible at configure time (#cmakedefine DFTFE_WITH_CLAP) with the original cuBLAS/hipBLAS/oneMKL/Fortran call sites preserved verbatim in #else branches, so a build without CLAP is bit-identical to upstream and CLAP itself stays an unmodified clone.

Isolated all CLAP headers in a single translation unit behind a CLAP-free shim header after discovering that CLAP redefines cuComplex, cudaMemcpyKind and cublasStatus_t in the global namespace and cannot coexist with the real vendor headers compiled by nvcc/hipcc/icpx.

Added a verification and measurement layer (reference dispatch, per-call numerical check on real DFT-FE call shapes, timing statistics incl. host-staging cost on the device path) so 'how well does DFT-FE run on CLAP' can be answered quantitatively; normalised ConjTrans to Trans for real operands and range-checked CLAP's cosmetic int64 interface.

projects.name: HYDRA: Hybrid Distributed Routing Architecture for All-Pairs Shortest Paths
projects.subtitle: MPI + OpenMP + CUDA blocked Floyd-Warshall with density-aware dispatch
projects.context: DS295 Parallel Programming course project (grade A+), IISc CDS teaching cluster
projects.one_liner: A heterogeneous MPI+OpenMP+CUDA blocked Floyd-Warshall APSP framework whose runtime density metric routes each 32x32 tile to GPU shared-memory kernels or INF-skipping CPU threads; benchmarked against 8 reimplemented published methods on identical hardware with bit-exact verification, reaching up to 90x over Sao et al.'s 2.5D algorithm and 54x GPU speedup over the blocked sequential baseline.

bullets.text: Designed and implemented HYDRA, a three-stage MPI+OpenMP+CUDA blocked Floyd-Warshall pipeline (MD vertex reordering and MPI_Scatterv row strips; per-pivot GPU Phase 1 + MPI_Ibcast pivot broadcast + concurrent GPU Phase 2/3 kernels and OpenMP sparse blocks; MPI_Gatherv and inverse permutation) on a 4-node SLURM cluster of Xeon Platinum 8352V (36 cores) + RTX A5000 nodes over 1 Gbps Ethernet.

Introduced density-aware dispatch: derived from a GPU warp-divergence vs CPU branch-prediction cost model that the optimal tile-density threshold lies in [0.08, 0.12], and confirmed rho = 0.10 empirically by sweeping {0.01..0.50} on the SNAP ca-HepPh graph (N = 12,008).

Reimplemented 8 published APSP methods (Sao 2.5D and supernodal, D'Andrea, Torgasin, Pradhan, Alghamdi, Kim, Takafuji) in C++/CUDA with identical flags on the same cluster and beat them by up to 90x (Sao 2.5D on ego-Facebook: 217.93 s vs 2.42 s), 26.7x (D'Andrea on ca-HepPh) and 4.1x (Kim's OpenMP, CPU-vs-CPU), while reporting the losses honestly (0.83x vs single-node Alghamdi at N = 4096).

Wrote 3-phase tiled CUDA kernels (32x32 thread blocks, three 4 KB shared-memory tiles, coalesced and bank-conflict-free, 100% shared-memory carve-out, two streams for async copies) that deliver 54.1x over the cache-blocked sequential baseline on a dense N = 4096 graph (12.35 s -> 0.228 s) and 49.6x at N = 1024.

Cut MPI broadcast volume up to 4x by CSR-packing sparse pivot rows (density < 25%), balanced scale-free graphs with degree-sorted round-robin MD reordering (3.5% gain on ca-HepPh), and verified every backend bit-exact against the sequential reference (zero mismatches on 6 configurations).

Profiled with TAU and Nsight Systems, attributing HYDRA's 2.9 s overhead vs pure OpenMP at N = 4096 entirely to MPI_Ibcast latency (about 0.5 ms per pivot) on 1 Gbps Ethernet, and confirmed GPU kernels overlap MPI broadcasts as designed.

projects.name: Parallel framework for face-wise (Hadamard) tensor product and slice-wise QR/SVD
projects.subtitle: Serial / OpenMP / CUDA / hybrid CPU+GPU backends with adaptive COO/ELL sparse storage
projects.context: DS285 Tensor Computations for Data Science course project (grade A), IISc teaching cluster; written as a preface to the thesis
projects.one_liner: Header-only C++17/CUDA framework for the face-wise product behind t-SVD and star-M algebra, with four execution backends, adaptive COO/ELL storage, density-aware path selection and cuBLAS batched GEMM; up to 18.66x over serial (OpenMP/hybrid) and 3.71x CUDA on dense 4000x4000x12, validated across a 700-run matrix.

bullets.text: Built a templated C++17/CUDA framework (Tensor3D, CooSlice, EllSlice, hybrid engine, CLI driver) for the face-wise product of third-order tensors and slice-wise QR (Modified Gram-Schmidt) and SVD (Jacobi eigen on A^T A) with serial, OpenMP, CUDA and hybrid CPU+GPU backends.

Implemented adaptive sparse storage (COO vs Sliced-ELLPACK chosen by slice density, 33x compression over dense at 1% density), density-aware dense/sparse path selection (threshold 0.18), work-weighted largest-first dynamic scheduling and cuBLAS cublasDgemmStridedBatched offload with the row-major transpose trick and 512 MiB adaptive batches.

Achieved up to 18.66x speedup over serial (hybrid, 5000x5000x100, 64 threads) and 3.71x with CUDA on a dense 4000x4000x12 tensor (2992.5 s -> 807.7 s) on a 36-core node with an RTX A5000, across a 700-run scalability matrix (7 sizes, 3 shapes, 4 modes, 1-72 threads).

Validated cross-mode correctness to 1e-6 for all density combinations, proved the serial path bitwise deterministic, and used Nsight Systems to show memory management takes >99% of CUDA API time on a small run (cudaMalloc 81%), pointing to device-memory pooling (projected ~5x).

projects.name: GPU longest common substring on 100-million-character strings
projects.subtitle: CUDA (prefix-doubling suffix array + Thrust radix sort) vs OpenMP (k-mer index + AVX2) vs serial SA-IS
projects.context: DS295 Parallel Programming Assignment 1, IISc CDS teaching cluster (Xeon Platinum 8352V 72 threads, RTX A5000 24 GB)
projects.one_liner: Longest common substring of two 10^8-character strings without the O(NM) DP table: evaluated three parallel formulations (binary search + double rolling hash, prefix-doubling suffix arrays, k-mer indexing + AVX2) and profiled the CPU memory wall; final CUDA version 3.17x faster than the best 72-thread OpenMP configuration.

bullets.text: Replaced the O(NM) dynamic-programming table (exabytes at N = 10^8) with O(N log N) formulations: binary search on length with double Rabin-Karp rolling hashes (collision probability about 1e-18), a Manber-Myers prefix-doubling suffix array, and a linear-time SA-IS + Kasai LCP serial baseline.

Wrote grid-stride CUDA hash kernels with coalesced writes and Thrust radix sort plus binary-search lookup kernels, achieving 29.55x over 36-thread OpenMP (32.5 s vs 961 s) for the rolling-hash formulation; profiled 80% of GPU time in thrust::sort.

Final methodology: CUDA prefix doubling with thrust::sort_by_key/scatter and an atomicMax LCP reduction ran in 0.649 s, 3.17x faster than the best OpenMP configuration (2.029 s, k-mer hash index + AVX2 _mm256_cmpeq_epi8 match extension), with 0.0029 s standard deviation across 30 trials.

Diagnosed the CPU memory wall: OpenMP efficiency fell from 100% at 16 threads to 26.5% at 64 threads because random k-mer hash lookups saturate memory bandwidth; ran 30 trials with 5 warm-ups instead of the requested 5 runs to get CLT-grade statistics.

projects.caution: Resume_IBM_app.txt and Resume_BioHack.txt describe this project with 'diagonal wavefront traversal', '40% GPU workload reduction', '22% initialization latency reduction' and 'billion-character'. None of these appear in the report; the report is 10^8 characters. Do not reuse those resume phrasings.

projects.name: OpenMP K-means clustering and MPI sparse matrix-vector multiplication
projects.subtitle: Shared-memory scheduling study and 128-process strong scaling on a 28M x 28M matrix
projects.context: DS221 Introduction to Scalable Systems assignment (report dated 18 Nov 2025; stored as Assignment 4, header says Assignment 3), IISc teaching cluster
projects.one_liner: Parallelised Lloyd's K-means with OpenMP (7.2x on 32 threads; showed dynamic scheduling is slower than serial) and built a balanced-nonzero MPI SpMV for the 27,993,600 x 27,993,600 NLPKKT240 matrix (760.6 M nonzeros) reaching 21.9x on 128 processes, with the memory-bandwidth plateau and load imbalance quantified.

bullets.text: Parallelised K-means (20,000 points, K = 20) with OpenMP parallel-for and reductions: 7.19x speedup on 32 threads with static scheduling (25.06 ms -> 3.49 ms) and identical centroids to the serial code, averaged over 30 runs.

Showed that dynamic scheduling with default chunk size made the parallel code slower than serial (0.39x) on a uniform workload, and used Amdahl/Gustafson/isoefficiency analysis to attribute the 16-to-32-thread plateau to a ~14% serial-equivalent fraction plus memory-bandwidth saturation.

Implemented MPI SpMV on the SuiteSparse NLPKKT240 matrix (27,993,600 rows, 760,648,352 nonzeros, ~12 GB) with balanced-nonzero row partitioning, per-rank parallel binary I/O via file offsets, MPI_Bcast of the 28 M-element vector and MPI_Gatherv of variable-size results.

Reached 21.90x strong-scaling speedup on 128 processes across six nodes, identified the single-node memory-bandwidth plateau (efficiency 0.367 -> 0.194 from 16 to 32 ranks) followed by 1.91x recovery on crossing to multiple nodes, and quantified load imbalance rising to 0.48 despite balanced FLOPs due to irregular cache/TLB behaviour.
Tuned OpenMPI byte-transfer layers (btl = self,vader,tcp; excluded unstable openib/ofi) to keep 64-128-rank runs stable on Ethernet.

projects.name: Air-B-N-C: Writing Your ABCs in Thin Air
projects.subtitle: Multi-modal air-writing character recognition with distributed edge inference and late sensor fusion
projects.date_note: Jan-Apr 2026 term course project; dataset session files are dated 2026-04-29
projects.context: CP330 Edge AI course project (grade B+), team of 3: Tathagata Ghosh, Amisha Sadhukhan, Gaurav Chaudhary
projects.repo_note: Repo name from BRIEF; URL returns HTTP 200 (checked 30 Sep 2026)
tech: Arduino Nano 33 BLE (nRF52840, LSM9DS1 IMU, PlatformIO/C++)
projects.one_liner: Touchless text input by writing characters in mid-air: a finger-worn IMU stream (TinyML decision-tree ensemble on GAF-encoded signals), a camera fingertip-trajectory branch (lightweight CNN with Ghost modules + ECA) and a ToF depth branch, each inferring at the edge and fused centrally with entropy-weighted late fusion over 62 alphanumeric classes (proposal).

bullets.text: Co-designed a three-modality architecture (IMU motion, RGB fingertip trajectory, ToF depth) where each edge device runs local inference and a central node performs entropy-weighted late fusion P = w1*P_IMU + w2*P_vision + w3*P_depth over 62 alphanumeric character classes.

IMU branch: Gramian Angular Field encoding of 6-axis time series with a forest of shallow decision trees on the sensor hub aggregated by bagging/boosting on the microcontroller; vision branch: rasterised (x, y) fingertip trajectories classified by a CNN with Ghost modules and Efficient Channel Attention; depth branch: 1D CNN / pruned LSTM on z(t).

Implemented the IMU firmware on an Arduino Nano 33 BLE (PlatformIO, ArduinoBLE + Arduino_LSM9DS1) with BLE-to-CSV collection scripts, and the vision-branch trajectory classifier trained in PyTorch with Optuna hyper-parameter search (baseline_fp32 / final_fp32 checkpoints) for inference on a Raspberry Pi 4.

Planned model compression for microcontroller deployment (INT8 post-training quantisation, magnitude pruning) and PyTorch DDP ring-all-reduce training with cross-modal contrastive alignment on the GPU cluster.

projects.name: Wrist-worn IMU human activity recognition on Nicla Vision
projects.subtitle: 60 Hz data pipeline, 126-feature windows, Optuna-tuned tree models and an accuracy-vs-memory deployment study
projects.one_liner: End-to-end TinyML HAR: MicroPython firmware streaming 6-axis IMU data at a drift-corrected 60 Hz over UDP, a Streamlit QA dashboard, 26,819 sliding windows x 126 features for 12 activities, Optuna-tuned decision tree (94.5% test accuracy) chosen over a 97.4% random forest because it fits in 135 KB as nested if-else rules.

bullets.text: Wrote MicroPython firmware for the Nicla Vision's LSM6DSOX (SPI) with a ticks-based drift-correction loop holding a strict 60 Hz sample rate, streaming timestamped 6-axis packets over a UDP hotspot link; built a Streamlit live-plot/record/playback dashboard for data QA and collected 5 minutes per activity for 12 activities.

Engineered 26,819 sliding windows (N = 20, 50% overlap) into 126-dimensional feature vectors (20 statistical, temporal, entropy and FFT features x 6 channels + 6 raw values) with balanced class weights for the imbalanced classes.

Compared five cross-validation strategies and Gini vs entropy splitting, tuned SVM/decision-tree/random-forest with Optuna, and selected a full-depth decision tree (94.48% test accuracy, macro-F1 0.933) over a 97.35% random forest because the tree is 134.9 KB versus ~14.8 MB.
Exported the chosen tree as nested if-else rules for direct embedding in the MicroPython firmware, leaving RAM for the interpreter and network stack.

bullets.text: Implemented Supervised Fine-Tuning from scratch in PyTorch (chain-of-thought prompt/response formatting, prompt-token causal masking with ignore_index, shifted cross-entropy, training/eval loops) for a <100M-parameter causal LM on math word problems.

projects.name: Multi-label classification and semantic segmentation on PASCAL VOC-style data
projects.subtitle: NumPy PCA, ResNet50 multi-scale head with Asymmetric Loss, ConvNeXt-Base + DeepLabV3+ with 12-pass TTA, Wilcoxon and bootstrap testing
projects.context: DS216 Machine Learning for Data Science, Assignment 2 (Kaggle leaderboard; report 16 Apr 2026; course grade B+)
projects.one_liner: Three-part vision pipeline: PCA from scratch in NumPy (170 of 3072 components explain 95% variance), a ResNet50 backbone with a custom 4-stage FPN-style head and Asymmetric Loss for 20-class multi-label classification (val F1@0.5 = 0.812, per-class thresholds), and a ConvNeXt-Base + DeepLabV3+ decoder for 21-class segmentation with Focal-Dice loss, CutMix and 12-pass multi-scale TTA, compared statistically with Wilcoxon signed-rank and bootstrap CIs.

bullets.text: Implemented PCA in pure NumPy on 2,200 images (32x32 RGB, d = 3072): 170 components capture 95% of variance and 506 capture 99%, a 94.5% dimensionality reduction.

Built a 20-class multi-label classifier: frozen-task ResNet50 feature extractor, 1x1 projections + GAP from all four stages concatenated into a 1024-d fused vector, 2-layer FC head, Asymmetric Loss with label smoothing, AdamW + CyclicLR, AMP; per-class threshold sweep lifted validation F1 (best val F1@0.5 = 0.812, 25.0M trainable params).

Built a 21-class semantic segmenter: ConvNeXt-Base (timm) backbone with a custom DeepLabV3+ decoder (6-branch ASPP at rates 6/12/18/24, auxiliary head, low-level skip), Focal-Dice loss, CutMix, 640 px inputs with gradient accumulation to effective batch 32 over 65 epochs, and 12-pass multi-scale flip TTA at inference (67.4M params).

Compared models with a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on 330 per-image mIoU scores (justified over the t-test by bounded, skewed scores) and a 1,000-sample bootstrap 95% CI on mIoU; packaged both models behind the mandated ClassificationModel/SegmentationModel API for Kaggle submission.

projects.one_liner: A CLI that samples a lecture video at a configurable rate, detects slide changes by grayscale pixel-difference ratio with a 5-frame stability tracker, drops near-duplicates by MSE similarity, lets the user review the extracted frames, and lays them out aspect-correct on A4 pages in a PDF; accepts local files or YouTube URLs.

bullets.text: Built a Python CLI (VideoProcessor / PDFGenerator) that samples frames at a configurable rate, downscales to grayscale, flags slide transitions when the changed-pixel ratio exceeds a threshold and the previous five frames were stable, and removes near-duplicates with an MSE similarity score (default 0.95).

Supported local videos and YouTube URLs (pytube download of the best progressive/adaptive mp4 stream), a manual review pause before PDF assembly, and aspect-ratio-preserving centring of each slide on an A4 page with fpdf.

site_copy.title: Tathagata Ghosh · HPC and GPU computing
site_copy.description: Tathagata Ghosh, M.Tech Computational and Data Science at IISc Bangalore: exact multi-GPU tensor decompositions in C++/CUDA, MPI and NCCL.

hero.kicker: HPC · GPU computing · M.Tech CDS, IISc Bangalore
hero.headline: I make tensors smaller and clusters busier.
lines: I am an M.Tech student in Computational and Data Science at IISc Bangalore (2025–2027). My thesis is tSVDm: exact multi-GPU tensor SVDs in C++/CUDA, MPI and NCCL, checked against the theorems they come from.
Before that: Data Science Intern at IBM (2026), and Software Engineer at RMES (2024–25), building C#/.NET software that monitors high-voltage electrical assets.

what.intro: The short version, with most of the Greek letters removed.
what.thesis: My thesis builds tSVDm, a distributed C++/CUDA implementation of two tensor decompositions: t-SVDM, which keeps the same rank in every slice, and t-SVDMII, which keeps whatever it takes to retain a chosen fraction of the total energy. It runs on 16 NVIDIA V100 GPUs across two nodes with MPI and NCCL, compresses large multi-dimensional data, and is exact rather than approximate: I checked its output against the published theorems instead of assuming it.
mproduct: Treat a 3-D tensor as a stack of matrices and mix that stack along its depth with an invertible matrix M (in tSVDm, the DCT-II), which turns one tangled 3-D problem into many independent matrices called frontal faces.

In that transformed space, multiplying two tensors is just multiplying matching faces, so each face gets an ordinary SVD and a truncation, and Eckart-Young-style optimality guarantees carry over from matrices.

The only step that couples the faces is the transform itself, so tSVDm spends most of its communication on exactly that step (an NCCL ring over NVLink) and lets 16 GPUs factorise faces independently the rest of the time.
what.practice: Day to day that means CUDA streams and kernels, NCCL and MPI communication, deciding where a 512 GB tensor should live when it does not fit in GPU memory, and benchmarking carefully enough to publish the cases where the GPU loses.

research.intro: One thesis, two nodes, sixteen GPUs, and a strong preference for answers that match the theorem.
research.application_setting: Application setting: POD-DEIM reduced-order modelling (Rao et al., Argonne National Laboratory).
highlights: Exact by design. Every frontal face gets an exact economy SVD (cuSOLVER gesvdj on concurrent CUDA streams), because t-SVDMII's threshold is a global order statistic that no randomized per-face shortcut can reproduce.
Checked against the theory. The energy identity holds to 8.7e-15 in FP64, and the Eckart-Young equalities of Theorems 10 and 11 match the measured reconstruction error to every printed digit in FP64.
Faster than an independent CPU/MPI reference by 1.5x to 8.8x end-to-end where frontal faces are 1024 or larger (8.76x at 4096×4096×64 in FP64), node for node, under a written fairness protocol.
Scales. Strong scaling on a 1024³ tensor: 7.89x on 8 GPUs and 14.20x on 16 GPUs in FP32, 15.77x on 16 GPUs in FP64. Weak-scaling efficiency 0.985 within one node.
Runs what the reference cannot. A 4096³ FP64 tensor (512 GB, plus 1 TB of factors) finishes in 2719 s on 16 GPUs through a host-staged out-of-core path; the same job OOM-kills the CPU reference.

Honest about the losses. On small faces the GPU runs at 0.23–0.86x of the reference because per-face solver launches cannot fill a V100, and the report quantifies that regime instead of cropping it out.

Read the paper closely. Documented two defects in the published pseudocode of Kilmer, Horesh, Avron and Newman (2019): a squared threshold compared against unsquared singular values, and a missing 1/|c|² factor in Theorem 11.
research.aside: My first full benchmark campaign measured a truncation that truncated nothing: the threshold compared local against global energy and never fired on more than one GPU. I rewrote it as a distributed bisection with one scalar Allreduce per step, and the threshold is now bit-identical on 1, 2, 4 and 8 GPUs.

site_copy.projects_intro: Course projects I treated like papers: reimplemented baselines, identical hardware, bit-exact checks, and the losing rows left in.

hydra.result: A hybrid MPI + OpenMP + CUDA all-pairs shortest-path solver that routes each tile to GPU or CPU by density: up to 90x faster than Sao et al.'s 2.5D algorithm (217.93 s to 2.42 s on ego-Facebook), 26.7x over D'Andrea, and 54.1x GPU speedup over the cache-blocked sequential baseline at N = 4096, with every backend verified bit-exact.
hydra.aside: For a fair comparison I reimplemented eight published APSP methods on the same cluster with identical flags. The table keeps the rows where HYDRA loses (0.83x against single-node Alghamdi at N = 4096).

tensor-hadamard.result: Header-only C++17/CUDA framework for the face-wise tensor product and slice-wise QR/SVD, with serial, OpenMP, CUDA and hybrid backends and adaptive COO/ELL storage: up to 18.66x over serial and 3.71x with CUDA on a dense 4000×4000×12 tensor, across a 700-run scalability matrix.
tensor-hadamard.aside: Nsight Systems showed cudaMalloc and cudaFree taking over 99% of CUDA API time on small runs: the GPU equivalent of spending the whole trip looking for parking.

lcs-gpu.context: DS295 Parallel Programming, Assignment 1, IISc, Feb 2026
lcs-gpu.result: Longest common substring of two 10<sup>8</sup>-character strings, where the textbook DP table would need exabytes: the final CUDA prefix-doubling version runs in 0.649 s, 3.17x faster than the best OpenMP configuration, with a 0.0029 s standard deviation over 30 trials.
lcs-gpu.aside: The assignment asked for 5 timing runs. I ran 30, plus 5 warm-ups, and cited the Central Limit Theorem to justify it.

dftfe-clap.result: Routed all eight xgemm overloads in DFT-FE's BLAS wrapper through the CLAP library behind a configure-time switch, added a verification and timing layer on real DFT-FE call shapes, and kept the CLAP-off build bit-identical to upstream.
dftfe-clap.aside: CLAP turned out to redefine cuComplex in the global namespace, so its headers now live alone in one translation unit behind a shim. Some headers need their own room.

kmeans-spmv.context: DS221 Introduction to Scalable Systems (grade A), IISc, Nov 2025
kmeans-spmv.result: MPI sparse matrix-vector multiply on the 27,993,600 × 27,993,600 NLPKKT240 matrix (760.6M nonzeros): 21.90x on 128 processes, with the memory-bandwidth plateau and a 0.48 load imbalance diagnosed. OpenMP K-means: 7.19x on 32 threads.
kmeans-spmv.aside: Also showed that OpenMP dynamic scheduling with the default chunk size can make parallel code slower than serial (0.39x). It is in the report, as a warning to others.

edgeai-imu.result: MicroPython firmware streaming 6-axis IMU data at a drift-corrected 60 Hz, 26,819 windows × 126 features for 12 activities, and an Optuna-tuned decision tree at 94.48% test accuracy (macro-F1 0.933).
edgeai-imu.aside: It beat a 97.35% random forest on the one metric the microcontroller cared about: 134.9 KB versus about 14.8 MB.

mlds-segmentation.more: A ResNet50 multi-label classifier (validation F1 of 0.812) and a ConvNeXt-Base + DeepLabV3+ segmenter, compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and bootstrap confidence intervals rather than by squinting at the leaderboard.

nlp-lm-rl.more: Supervised fine-tuning, DPO and GRPO implemented from scratch in PyTorch for a sub-100M-parameter model on math word problems.

air-b-n-c.more: Team of three: write characters in mid-air, and IMU, camera and depth branches each infer on the edge before a central node fuses them (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, PyTorch, Optuna).

video2pdf.more: A command-line tool that turns lecture recordings into deduplicated slide PDFs with OpenCV frame-change detection, written because the recordings were unusable as study material.

rag-k8s.more: Self-directed: a microservices retrieval-augmented generation platform on Kubernetes with vLLM inference, Qdrant vector search, Kafka ingestion, Istio mTLS and Prometheus, Grafana and Jaeger observability.

upi-fraud.more: Self-directed: a GPU fraud-detection pipeline for UPI-style payments with RAPIDS cuDF XGBoost, Dask preprocessing, Ray Tune search and MLflow tracking.

ott-recsys.more: Self-directed: a hybrid recommender (collaborative filtering, content embeddings, neural ranking) trained with PyTorch DDP.

logic-locking-alu.more: B.Tech project (Part II graded A+): XOR/XNOR logic locking against hardware-Trojan insertion in a 16-bit ALU, with Cadence Genus and Tempus analysis to find the likely insertion sites.
